The fabrication of suspended sub-100 nm Si NWs

Abstract
Silicon nanowires (Si NWs) are versatile one-dimensional building blocks for gas and biochemical sensors, MEMS/NEMS
physical transduction platforms, and integrated electronic devices because of their high surface-to-volume ratios and
compatibility with semiconductor processing. A key limitation of conventional top-down fabrication is its reliance on
furnace-based high-temperature steps, such as thermal oxidation and LPCVD, which can induce residual stress and
constrain post-CMOS integration because of thermal-budget limits above 400 °C. Here, we present a furnace-free, low-

thermal-budget fabrication approach for suspended Si NWs with a maximum process temperature of 180 °C. The
process forms suspended Si NWs at the top surface of both bulk Si substrates and SOI substrates with a 2 µm device
layer. The method deﬁnes a nanoscale Si surface protrusion and uses a conformal Cr sidewall coating to preserve
linewidth during DRIE release. The process yields suspended Si NWs with critical dimensions down to 50 nm, aspect
ratios of up to 100, and array pitches of 5 µm, while supporting integration into junctionless ﬁeld-effect transistor
architectures. Electrical measurements conﬁrm ohmic behavior in two-terminal NW devices and demonstrate

From an application perspective, the usefulness of a
suspended Si NW fabrication route is determined not
only by the minimum achievable linewidth, but also by
how well the process satisﬁes the manufacturing con-
straints imposed by the target device class. In biochemical
and gas-sensing applications, the NW surface must
remain accessible for post-fabrication functionalization,
catalytic decoration, or selective metallization, while the
suspended geometry can reduce substrate interactions
and improve thermal or electrical isolation11,17,28,29. In
MEMS/NEMS physical sensors, Si NWs are commonly
used as piezoresistive or resonant transduction elements
coupled to larger microstructures; therefore, deterministic
alignment, robust anchoring, and monolithic integration
